title: How to Vet a Zendrop Supplier Before You Commit Ad Spend
excerpt: A supplier vetting checklist to run before you scale ad spend: sample shipping tests, stock signal checks, a communication test, and margin math that assumes refunds happen.
body: Ad spend is an amplifier. Whatever is true about a supplier at fifty orders a month becomes ten times more visible at five hundred, which is why vetting belongs before the scaling decision and not after it. The goal of a supplier review is not to find a perfect partner. It is to find the failure modes you can tolerate, price them into your margin, and avoid the ones that generate tickets faster than your team can answer them.

Order the product yourself using the exact shipping option you plan to sell. Not the fastest option, not the one the dashboard highlights, but the one your customer will receive. Record three numbers: processing time before the label is created, transit time, and the gap between the first scan and the last update. A supplier that ships in two days but sits on the label for three produces the same angry tickets as a slow carrier.

Test the stock signal instead of trusting it. Put a variant-heavy product on your store, sell a few units, and watch how quickly available counts move on the supplier side, including across a weekend. Then ask how inventory updates propagate and what happens when stock runs out mid-fulfillment. You want an answer that names a mechanism and a timeline, not a reassurance, because overselling is the shortest path to refunds and disputes.

Run a communication test with a realistic scenario. Send a question about an address change and a damaged delivery, then measure both the response time and the quality of the reply. Policy quoted back at you shows what escalations will feel like in peak season. A reply naming the fix, the timeline, and who absorbs the cost shows the account is backed by someone who has handled it before.

Look at what the customer actually receives. Packaging, inserts, branding, and whether an invoice with a supplier price lands inside the box are all part of the product experience. If unboxing is part of your brand promise, confirm what can be customized and what the minimum is, then verify it with the sample rather than a screenshot. Discovering a plain mailer after promising a branded unboxing in your ad creative is an expensive way to learn.

Finish with margin math that assumes things go wrong. Add landed cost, shipping, payment fees, and a refund allowance of at least ten percent for a new SKU, then check whether contribution margin still supports your target acquisition cost. Scale only the products that clear the bar under that assumption. The ones that only work at a zero percent refund rate are not profitable products, they are optimistic forecasts that push risk onto support.

The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, which is a useful baseline before you run this checklist. The Zendrop profile at /tool/zendrop covers the supplier tooling and automation it offers, so you can confirm which parts of the vetting work the platform already does for you.
